geometry_section:
# Geometry and user-side layout
- Preserve {product_image}'s exact framing. The product may be small or off-center and
  need not dominate the image. Never shrink it to reveal furniture; crop the
  furniture at the frame instead.
- The support's width and depth axes follow axis_angle_deg. Rectangular edges
  follow those axes; round and oval rims curve within the same support plane.
  Parallel 3D edges share vanishing points and need not look parallel on-screen.
  All room objects share one floor plane and consistent horizon; align furniture,
  not the product.
- A printer sits square on its support: its front and side faces are parallel
  in 3D to the support's width and depth axes, and therefore to the edges of a
  rectangular top. Estimate its axis_angle_deg from the two bottom edges meeting
  at the base corner nearest the camera (front bottom edge = width axis, side
  bottom edge = depth axis), not from the top, trays or control panel. In a
  frontal view, the visible front bottom edge is the width axis.
- A laptop need not sit exactly square to its desk; the desk follows the
  laptop's estimated chassis yaw. Other products share their chassis axes with
  the support.
- Identify the user side from the screen, control panel or output tray.
  Put working seating where a user would face the screen. A screen facing away
  from the camera requires the working chair across the table, not behind the
  lid in the foreground. For a printer allow standing access; do not invent a
  dedicated printer chair. Other requested office chairs belong at workstations.
- Keep the support category from the original request. For printers, when the
  category is unspecified, choose a credible substantial cabinet, low credenza,
  fitted counter or dedicated equipment table. A requested printer table is a
  substantial dedicated equipment table, not a person's occupied workstation
  desk. A cabinet, credenza or fitted counter normally has a rectangular top,
  but must retain its described furniture body; support_top_shape specifies
  only the top outline, not the furniture category.
- For laptops, keep user_edge_gap_m small so the laptop sits near the support's
  user-facing boundary. For a round or oval top, measure this gap along the selected user-side axis
  (width for width_left/width_right, depth for near_camera/far_from_camera) to the user-facing rim point aligned with the
  product center, not to an invented straight side. Keep the gap modest while
  allowing the entire product base to fit inside the curved rim.
- There is no tabletop beyond the user-facing edge or curved rim. When user_side
  is near_camera, that region is in the lower frame: plan what fills it, such as
  the support's front boundary, the working chair or floor, instead of extending
  the support toward the camera.
- Arrange a believable lifestyle scene as if someone has just stepped away
  from using the product, with no person shown. Plan furniture orientation
  and spacing together: leave realistic room to sit or stand, reach the
  product and requested supplies, and operate it without obstructions.
  Adapt furniture to the fixed product; do not add props merely to suggest use
  or add extra devices.
- Supply the structured "geometry" required by the schema: estimated camera
  height, support height, look-at height, horizontal distance, vertical FOV,
  support yaw, support_top_shape, support width/depth, product base footprint,
  user side, user-edge gap, support lateral offset and furniture boxes. Describe
  the same support placement in composition and the final prompt.
- Downward pitch is derived as
  atan((camera_height_m - look_at_height_m) / horizontal_distance_m).
  Use zero camera roll. Do not independently choose a conflicting tilt or lens:
  the code derives a rectilinear focal estimate from FOV and canvas aspect.
- Use camera height above support height, look-at height between them, positive
  horizontal distance, vertical FOV from 10 to 100 degrees, and support yaw
  strictly between -75 and 75 degrees.
- Choose axis_angle_deg from chassis/screen/front edges, not an oval base.
  Positive yaw means the width axis's right end is farther away; negative means
  nearer. On-screen depth also depends on off-center product framing. The guide
  supplies actual projected directions; do not infer them from yaw sign alone.
- Support and footprint sizes are construction estimates. Shape choice must
  not change the product footprint or original pixel bounds. The code places
  the support around the product base from user_side, user_edge_gap_m and
  support_lateral_offset_m, and the guide draws its actual outline. Keep the
  user's requested support type and shape.
- Set support_top_shape to rectangular, round or oval. Rectangular retains the
  existing rectangular construction and gap/offset meanings. For round,
  support_width_m and support_depth_m are equal physical diameters. For oval,
  they are unequal physical diameters along the support's width and depth axes.
  Round and oval tops are projected ellipses in the same support plane and
  camera, not rectangles with rounded corners. Use the requested shape; when
  unspecified, retain the existing rectangular default.

- For round and oval tops, all four product-base corners must lie inside the
  ellipse; checking only the center or a rectangular bounding box is not enough.
  Choose physically normal support dimensions and modest gap and lateral offset.
  support_lateral_offset_m must leave clearance for the full footprint width
  and the curved rim. Fit the support around the unchanged product, never move,
  rotate or resize the product or alter its footprint to make it fit.
- Printers normally stand against a wall: set back_edge_against_wall true unless
  the original request clearly places the printer away from walls. Keep the
  existing printer-to-wall placement policy. Round and oval laptop tables are
  often freestanding; do not impose wall adjacency merely because a support
  is present.
- Describe the actual visible boundary: straight edges and visible corners for
  rectangular tops, curved rims and visible arcs for round or oval tops. A fixed
  crop may show only an arc. Do not widen the camera, change framing or demand
  a full circle, full perimeter or visible furniture base to prove the shape.
- Furniture boxes are visible [left, top, right, bottom] bounds normalized to
  0-1, with positive area and no overlap with fixed product bounds. Use
  working_seat for user-side working chairs, background_furniture for others.
  Each working_seat box area must be at most 1.5 times the product box area.
  Move seating deeper or crop it rather than enlarging a foreground chair.
- {guide_image} will be a geometry-only diagram, not a photographic reference.
  Never reproduce its lines, labels, bounds or flat guide colors.

constant_replacements._GEOMETRY_ONLY:
THIS CALL PLANS GEOMETRY ONLY. Return only geometry and product_category. Camera text, composition, the image prompt, materials and scale notes are written in a later call after the geometry guide is drawn.

SUPPORT PLAUSIBILITY: The support must be real furniture that people actually use to hold this product in this kind of room, standing where such furniture normally stands. The requested support type names the furniture; it does not fix its size. Keep that category and its body: a cabinet, credenza or fitted counter does not become a table because its top is rectangular. For a printer with no specified support category, choose a credible substantial cabinet, low credenza, fitted counter or dedicated equipment table. A requested printer table is a substantial dedicated equipment table, not a person's occupied workstation desk; allow standing access and unobstructed operation. Choose support_width_m, support_depth_m and support_height_m typical for that furniture and for using this product: the top is only as deep as such furniture normally is while still holding the product's whole base, and the height suits how people reach and use the product. Set back_edge_against_wall true when that furniture would normally stand against a wall in this room; the wall then stands at the support's rear boundary, never through its top. Printers normally stand against a wall: for a printer, set back_edge_against_wall true unless the original user request clearly places it away from walls. The wall can never stand between camera and product. Round or oval laptop tables are often freestanding; set back_edge_against_wall false unless the original request or normal placement of the requested furniture calls for wall adjacency. Secondary furniture in furniture_boxes stands beside, behind or in front of the support, never inside it.

SUPPORT SHAPE: Set support_top_shape to rectangular, round or oval, retaining the requested top shape. When shape is unspecified, retain the existing rectangular default. Printer cabinets, credenzas, fitted counters and equipment tables normally have rectangular tops. The shape field describes only the top outline, not the furniture category. Rectangular retains the existing construction and gap/offset meanings. For round, support_width_m and support_depth_m are equal physical diameters; for oval, they are unequal physical diameters. The guide must project the ellipse in the same support plane and camera. All four unchanged product-base corners must lie inside the ellipse. Choose physically normal dimensions and modest gap and lateral offset; leave full footprint-width and curved-rim clearance. For round and oval tops, user_edge_gap_m is measured along the selected user-side axis (width for width_left/width_right, depth for near_camera/far_from_camera) to the user-facing rim point aligned with the product center, not to an invented straight side. Keep the product footprint, original pixel bounds, orientation, position and size fixed. Do not widen the camera or require a complete perimeter or visible furniture base: the fixed crop may show only an arc.
constant_replacements._PRIORITY:
STAGE B. Geometry is already fixed and drawn in Image 1 around the real product, at the exact Image 3 framing. Do not change it.

PRIORITY ORDER (strict):
1. The product (its real pixels in Image 1; Image 3 shows the same product on white for detail): its pixel position, size, orientation and visibility. Never move, resize, rotate, crop or occlude it.
2. The FIXED GEOMETRY (Image 1 and the text below): support top shape and orientation, the user-facing edge or curved rim and its position in the frame, the product-to-boundary distance, how far the top extends to each side, frame crop and camera.
3. The original user request. It chooses the room, support category and body, material, props, lighting, palette and mood. Its requested top shape is resolved in Stage A; do not redraw the fixed outline in Stage B.

When the user request asks for a different layout, extent, emphasis, framing, focal point, product size, or a table that fills or dominates the foreground, drop that part and follow 1 and 2. Your camera, composition and prompt must describe exactly the geometry of Image 1: the same support top shape and orientation, the user-facing boundary identified by user_side on the gray support area, top surface only on the drawn support, nothing beyond its user-facing boundary, props on the drawn top at plausible scale beside the product, and nothing occluding the product. Describe straight edges and visible corners only for rectangular tops; describe curved rims and visible arcs for round or oval tops. Both round and oval physical tops project as ellipses, so use support_top_shape to name the physical shape and Image 1 to describe its projection. A cropped arc is sufficient; do not demand the full perimeter or furniture base or change the camera to reveal them. Keep the original support category beneath the fixed top: a rectangular cabinet, credenza or fitted-counter top is not an instruction to replace its body with a table. Keep the user side and operating access.

WRITE IN PLAIN VISUAL WORDS. The image model follows pictures and plain descriptions, not measurements. Use the numbers below only to choose your words. In layout, camera, composition and prompt, describe sizes, distances, angles and positions the way a photographer briefs a set builder: by comparison with the product, the frame edges and nearby objects (for example "the tabletop continues about two laptop widths to the left of the laptop and a little less to the right", "the tabletop is about three times as deep as the laptop", "the table ends inside the frame on both sides", "the curved rim exits the frame on the left", "camera at standing eye height, looking gently down").

FIXED GEOMETRY (derived by code from Image 1):
constant_replacements._WRITE_OVERRIDE:
STAGE B OVERRIDE: geometry is a fixed input in this call, not an output. Image 1 is the drawn geometry guide and is visible to you now. Follow the PRIORITY ORDER in the user message: product first, fixed geometry second, user request third. Return layout, camera, composition and prompt, each written in plain visual words. layout opens the image prompt as its GEOMETRY section: short lines on the support's physical top shape, how its axes are turned and how its straight edges or curved rim run across the frame; which boundary faces the user and where it sits relative to the product; how close the product sits to that boundary, using the rim point aligned with the product center for a round or oval top; how much top surface continues on each side of the product and how deep the support is compared with the product; which ends and corners stay inside the frame for a rectangular top, or which arcs are visible or cropped for a round or oval top; the camera height and how steeply it looks down; and the product unchanged in its place. Do not invent straight sides or four corners for a curved top, or require its full perimeter or furniture base to be visible. Keep the support category and body from the original request, not from the shape field: a cabinet, credenza or fitted counter remains that furniture beneath its drawn top. Preserve user-side access, including standing operating access for printers.

IMAGE MODEL INPUT: the image model receives ONLY Image 1 and your text. It never sees the style reference or the product on white. In layout, camera, composition and prompt, never mention any image other than Image 1, the reference, or where a style or material came from. Describe the lighting, palette, materials and textures you take from the style reference directly in words, as a brief for a photographer who has never seen it. Never explain where a color, material or blue carrier was adapted or transferred from. Product detail comes from the real product pixels in Image 1.
constant_replacements._PRINTER_WALL: Printers normally stand against a wall: for a printer, set back_edge_against_wall true unless the original user request clearly places it away from walls.
constant_replacements._WRITE_PRINTER_WALL: PRINTER AGAINST THE WALL: the printer's back stands right against the wall at the support's back edge, with no gap, shelf or objects between them. State this plainly in the prompt.
constant_replacements._LEGEND: Image 1 is the canvas to edit: a geometry-only diagram at the final framing whose product pixels are the real product. Keep those product pixels unchanged. The flat gray area with a thin darker outline is the exact top surface of the support: the top covers exactly that area, with its boundary where the gray area's boundary is; the gray is not its color. Rectangular tops have straight edges; round and oval tops have projected elliptical rims, which the frame may crop to visible arcs. Use the fixed support_top_shape to distinguish a physically round top from an oval one, not its apparent projected proportions. Do not replace curved boundaries with straight sides or four corners, or widen the view to reveal the full outline or furniture base. The outline specifies the top, not the furniture category: retain the cabinet, credenza, fitted counter, equipment table or other support body described in the original request. Replace everything else in Image 1, including the white background and the gray fill, with the photographic scene. Never render any diagram mark.
constant_replacements._FINAL_CHECK: Final check before rendering: the product pixels, footprint, position, size and orientation are unchanged; the support top shape and orientation, user-facing edge or curved rim, product-to-boundary distance and top extent match the GEOMETRY section and Image 1. For round or oval tops, describe the actual visible arcs rather than straight sides or four corners, and measure the user-edge gap at the rim point aligned with the product center. Do not change the camera or crop to show the full perimeter or furniture base. The support category and body still match the original request; a rectangular top has not turned a cabinet, credenza or fitted counter into a table. Keep user-side and operating access, standing access for printers, shared perspective, and no extra people or devices. Where other scene text conflicts, follow GEOMETRY, with unchanged product pixels always first.

change_notes: Adds support_top_shape = rectangular/round/oval. Rectangular construction stays unchanged; round uses equal physical diameters and oval unequal diameters, projected in the existing support plane and camera.

Curved tops require all four fixed product-base corners inside the ellipse, normal furniture dimensions, modest gap/offset and lateral curvature clearance. The user-edge gap is measured at the user-facing rim point aligned with the product center.

Stage B describes the actual outline, distinguishing physical shape from projected appearance. Cropped arcs are valid; no new camera widening, full-perimeter or furniture-base display requirement is introduced.

Support category remains source-driven. Printer cabinets, low credenzas and fitted counters retain their bodies; requested printer tables are substantial dedicated equipment tables with standing access, not occupied personal desks.

Wall anchoring now applies to the printer support rather than forcing the printer chassis against the wall. Freestanding curved laptop tables are not automatically wall-backed. The existing Boolean wall flag still cannot encode an independent support-to-wall gap.

These prompts depend on matching schema, ellipse projection, rim-gap placement, all-four-corner validation and Stage B geometry-description updates. Prompt text alone cannot make a rectangular-only guide curved, and Stage B must not redraw an incorrectly planned guide.

Original writer inputs must supply café-round choices, cross-scene shape variety and printer category variety. These replacements do not revise the 160 writer prompts or guarantee batch-level distribution; previously all-table printer inputs will not become cabinets merely through the shape field.

Proposal only, pending approval to depart from the earlier same-pipeline constraint. The paused x-y movement experiment is excluded. Product orientation, position, size, footprint and original bounds remain fixed; no changes are proposed to model, blue policy, input references, unrelated room/object policy, rich CTech aesthetics, source-first ranking or camera contract. No deployment or image testing is claimed.
root_review_notes: Rejected Astra printer-chassis wall-clearance change as unrelated to shape/category and conflicting with earlier customer feedback; both wall constants remain pinned verbatim.
Rejected new unspecified-shape defaults: retain rectangular default when input does not specify shape; V6.2 writer owns diverse explicit shape choices.
Corrected rim gap direction: selected user-side axis, not universally support depth.
Other system sections/model/blue/position/orientation/size/camera contracts unchanged. Candidate only, no deployment or image test.
